topic.title: Classicism
topic.framework: The fixed base is Bacon and Dorr’s Classicism (C) in their relational type system. Types are generated from e and t by forming sigma→tau when tau is not e; every non-base type therefore ends in t. C is the smallest H-theory containing Logical Equivalence (Classicism, §1.3): lambda abstractions of H-equivalent formulas are identical. Preserve the theoremhood side condition; equivalence under optional assumptions does not satisfy it.
topic.notation: All type schemata use the fixed relational type system. Types and application associate to the right; curried application is parenthesized. Box applies after closing object variables. See Background for definitions and schema side conditions.

papers.title: Arithmetic is Necessary
papers.citation: Goodsell, Zachary William Lee. Arithmetic is Necessary. Draft dated 5 June 2024, 28 pages. Derives the necessity of arithmetic in the logic HKC (H plus K plus Countable Boolean Completeness) and shows that Boolean Completeness is inconsistent with the maximalization of any recursively enumerable extension of HK consistent with I, answering the question of Classicism, §2.6. Locators refer to this draft.

principles.name: Actual Profile
principles.statement: Every finite tuple has a true relational profile entailing every relation it instantiates; the tuple may be empty.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall\bar x\, .\,\exists Y\, .\,Y[\bar x]\land\forall Z\, .\,Z[\bar x]\to Y\le Z$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, n. 31, p. 25.

principles.name: Actuality
principles.statement: There is a true proposition that entails every true proposition.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 25.

principles.name: Atomicity
principles.statement: Every non-bottom entity of each relational type has an atom below it.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\tau\ne e\, .\,\forall x^\tau\, .\,x\le_\tau\neg_\tau x\lor\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)\land y\le_\tau x$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 24.

references.note: Bacon states the same principle as the Weak Leibniz Biconditionals, with weak worlds in place of atoms, and notes that Classicism calls its substantive direction Atomicity.

changes.summary: Added the alias Weak Leibniz Biconditionals and a reference to Bacon’s 2024 book; the statement is unchanged.

principles.name: Axiom of Infinity (type e)
principles.statement: There are not finitely many individuals. No finite cardinality holds of the universal property, so the domain of the type cannot be exhausted by finitely many steps from the empty property.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.

references.note: The draft's informal infinity claim, which the map had recorded only in its schematic form.

principles.notes: See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$. The quantified form is what is normally meant by an axiom of infinity. It implies the schema of the same name, and the converse fails by a compactness argument, so the two are kept as separate principles. Possible Infinity (type e), this axiom under a diamond, is recorded as a separate principle.

principles.name: Boolean Completeness
principles.statement: Every property of entities of a relational type has a greatest lower bound in that type.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, pp. 23–24.

principles.name: Boolean Completeness (type t)

principles.statement: The converse of Witnessed Possibility, with precisely the same formula, type and constant side conditions.

principles.name: Countable Boolean Completeness
principles.statement: Every countable property of entities of a relational type has a least upper bound in that type, where a property is countable when it injects into the natural numbers.
sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, §3.1, eq. (10), p. 8; Definition 6, p. 13.

references.note: The source states the principle for property types $\sigma t$ with least upper bounds; the map ranges over every relational type, as its Boolean Completeness does, and takes the source's parameters $\nu$, $0$ and successor to be $(et)t$, $\mathbf{0}_e$ and $\operatorname{Suc}_e$.

principles.notes: See Background for $\operatorname{Ctbl}$ and $\operatorname{LUB}$. The restriction of Boolean Completeness to countable properties; the least-upper-bound form is used to match the source, and is equivalent in C to a greatest-lower-bound form, since the pointwise negation of a countable property is countable. The source's hypothesis that the properties form a countably complete Boolean algebra modulo necessary equivalence. It suffices for the Necessity of Arithmetic and is therefore incompatible with Maximalist Classicism.

principles.name: ND
principles.statement: Distinct things of any type are necessarily distinct.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–22.

principles.name: ND (type t)
principles.statement: ND (type t) in the displayed closed propositional formulation.

principles.name: Distinctness-preserving collapse
principles.statement: Every truth is necessary under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix E, p. 83.

principles.name: Distinctness (pure)
principles.statement: Every closed pure identity not provable in C is false. The non-theorem condition is metalinguistic.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.4, pp. 35–36.
principles.notes: The reference theory in the side condition is the fixed background C.

principles.name: Distinctness (signature Σ)
principles.statement: The Distinctness schema for the fixed nonlogical signature Sigma.
principles.formal: $A\ne B\quad(A=B\text{ closed in }\mathcal L(\Sigma);\ C(\Sigma)\nvdash A=B)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 37–39.

principles.name: Existence
principles.statement: Every type is inhabited.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.1, p. 7.

principles.name: Extensionality
principles.statement: At each relational type, coextensive relations are identical; include the nullary propositional case.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X Y\, .\,(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])\to X=Y$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16.

principles.name: Fregean Axiom
principles.statement: Materially equivalent propositions are identical.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16.

principles.name: Functional Choice
principles.statement: Every serial binary relation admits a selecting operation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

principles.name: Functionality
principles.statement: Operations with the same value on every argument are identical. The output type is relational.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16, especially n. 18.

principles.name: Gallin Extensional Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation is coextensive with one that is persistent and has a persistent pointwise negation. This is the source’s comparison with Gallin’s different rigidity convention.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\exists Y\, .\,\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land\operatorname{Persistent}(\neg Y)\land(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 37, p. 28.

references.locator: p. 77, as described in Classicism n. 37

principles.name: General Separated Structure
principles.statement: Let a_1…a_n and b_1…b_m be constants of Sigma, possibly with repetitions, none occurring in the closed terms F and G, and let pi be a bijection from variables x_1…x_k to the distinct constants among them. If F applied to the a’s equals G applied to the b’s, then abstracting the constants yields identical pure-position operations.
principles.formal: $F a_1\cdots a_n=G b_1\cdots b_m\to\lambda\bar x\, .\,F(\pi a_1)\cdots(\pi a_n)=\lambda\bar x\, .\,G(\pi b_1)\cdots(\pi b_m)\quad(a_i,b_j\text{ constants of }\Sigma,\text{ none in the closed }F,G;\ \pi\text{ a bijection from }\bar x\text{ to the distinct ones})$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §4, p. 565.
principles.notes: Bacon’s instances: Rab = Sba implies R and S are converses; Rab = Fb implies R forgets its first argument; Raa = Fa implies F is the reflexivization of R. Equivalent in C to Separated Structure by the recorded results.

principles.name: NI
principles.statement: Identity is necessary at every type.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, p. 22.

principles.name: Independence (signature Σ)
principles.statement: No constant of Sigma is a pure operation applied to other constants: for a closed pure term A and distinct constants c, d_1,…,d_n with n ≥ 0, c differs from A applied to the d’s. With n = 0, no constant denotes a pure entity.
principles.formal: $c\ne A\,d_1\cdots d_n\quad(A\text{ closed and pure};\ c,d_1,\ldots,d_n\text{ distinct constants};\ n\ge0)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §4, p. 568 and n. 53.
principles.notes: Bacon’s independence of the fundamental, read for the constants of a fundamental language; his n. 53 derives it from Logical Necessity. The constant c has a relational type, since the applied term does.

principles.name: Inextensible Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a inextensible one.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\exists Y\, .\,\operatorname{Inextensible}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 38, p. 29.

principles.name: Infinity Schema (type e)
principles.statement: There are arbitrarily many pairwise distinct entities of this fixed type; one sentence for each positive integer n.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.
principles.notes: Schema-level reading of the source’s informal infinity claim; no choice-dependent equivalence with Dedekind infinity is assumed. One sentence for each n, so it is weaker than the quantified Axiom of Infinity (type e), which implies it. The converse fails by a compactness argument, which the map does not yet witness with a model.

changes.summary: Renamed from “Infinity (type e)” to mark it as the schema, now that the quantified Axiom of Infinity (type e) is recorded separately. The id, the statement and every connection are unchanged.

principles.name: Intensionality

principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X Y\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])\to X=Y$

principles.name: Logical Necessity
principles.statement: The Logical Necessity schema: necessity at distinct matching constants is equivalent to universal truth of the pure-formula. Preserve the side conditions of Witnessed Possibility.
principles.formal: $\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\leftrightarrow(\forall\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$

principles.name: Modal Freedom (signature Σ)
principles.statement: For pure formulas P and Q with free variables among the disjoint tuples x and y, and distinct constants c and d of matching types, if P is possible at c and Q is possible at d then P and Q are jointly possible there.
principles.formal: $\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\land\Diamond Q[\bar d/\bar y]\to\Diamond(P[\bar c/\bar x]\land Q[\bar d/\bar y])\quad(P,Q\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x\text{ resp. }\bar y;\ \bar c\bar d\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §3, pp. 556–557, principle (5) and its generalization.
principles.notes: Bacon’s formalization of Schaffer’s Modal Freedom, stated for two distinct constants R and S of a fundamental language. The instance with no constants is equivalent to No Pure Contingency.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of B. Type quantifiers and formula side conditions remain outside the box.

principles.statement: Every closed instance of 5 is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of 5. Type quantifiers and formula side conditions remain outside the box.

principles.name: □Plenitude
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Plenitude is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Plenitude. Type quantifiers and formula side conditions remain outside the box.

principles.name: □Relational Choice
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Relational Choice is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Relational Choice}$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.
Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.4, pp. 175–176.

references.note: □Functional Choice is the principle valid in the Gallin and Williamson models, from which Bacon and Dorr derive S5, the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals, Rigid Comprehension and Boolean Completeness.

principles.notes: Added at Cian Dorr’s request on 22 September 2026, after the coalesced roots showed Relational Choice holding at a root while failing at accessible worlds.

principles.name: □Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Rigid Comprehension is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Rigid Comprehension}$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Rigid Comprehension. Type quantifiers and formula side conditions remain outside the box.

principles.name: □Strong Leibniz Biconditionals
principles.statement: Every closed instance of the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the type range.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals}$
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 166, 169–170.
principles.notes: The boxed form is the one Theorem 8.2 of the book connects with □BF and □Atomicity. Since strong worlds are only required to be possible, not necessarily possible, the unboxed form does not yield 5; Exercise 8.13 shows that requiring necessarily weak worlds does.

principles.name: □Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t)
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t) is necessary.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t)}$
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–166.

principles.name: □Tractarianism
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Tractarianism is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Tractarianism. Type quantifiers and formula side conditions remain outside the box.

principles.name: Necessity of Arithmetic
principles.statement: Every arithmetical sentence is either necessarily true or necessarily false, given that possibly zero is not a successor and successor is injective on numbers. One sentence for each arithmetical sentence.
sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, eq. (1), p. 2; Definition 8 and Theorem 9, pp. 19–21.

references.locator: eq. (1), p. 2; Definition 8 and Theorem 9, pp. 19–21
references.note: The source's necessity schema, with its parameters $\nu$, $0$ and successor taken to be $(et)t$, $\mathbf{0}_e$ and $\operatorname{Suc}_e$, so that its natural numbers are the finite cardinalities of individuals.

principles.notes: See Background for $I$ and for arithmetical sentences. The antecedent $I$ is needed because the axioms of arithmetic are not theorems of C: with one individual the second numeral is the empty cardinality, so successor is not injective. In C the first conjunct of $I^*$ is a theorem, so $I$ amounts to the possible injectivity of $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ on finite cardinalities, which Possibility (pure) grants. Each instance is a closed pure sentence, so the schema follows from No Pure Contingency; it follows in C from Countable Boolean Completeness, and it is incompatible with Possibility (pure) by Gödel's first incompleteness theorem.

principles.name: No Contingency (signature Σ)
principles.statement: Each closed sentence of the language of the fixed signature Sigma, if true, is necessary. A sentence schema, standing to No Pure Contingency as Possibility (signature Σ) stands to Possibility (pure).
principles.formal: $P\to\Box P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 27 (No Pure Contingency).

references.note: The pure schema of which this is the signature version.

principles.notes: Holds in every one-world model whatever the constants denote, so it is consistent; but it is incompatible with Witnessed Possibility and hence with Logical Necessity, Separated Structure and Maximalist Classicism for Σ: a constant of relational type is possibly top and possibly not top under Witnessed Possibility, while this schema makes whichever obtains necessary.

principles.name: No Pure Contingency
principles.statement: Each closed sentence of the pure language, if true, is necessary. This is a sentence schema, not a quantifier over propositions.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 27.

references.locator: Logical Foundations of Philosophy; cited in Classicism p. 27

references.note: The empty-tuple instance of Logical Necessity.

changes.summary: Added a reference to Logical Combinatorialism; the statement is unchanged.

principles.name: Ordinary Comprehension
principles.statement: Every well-typed formula P with distinguished variables y defines a coextensive relation; X is fresh, and any other free object variables are universally closed.
principles.formal: $\exists X\, .\,\forall\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\leftrightarrow P\quad(P\text{ a formula in which }X\text{ is not free})$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, p. 27.

changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

principles.name: Persistent Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a persistent one.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\exists Y\, .\,\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 38, p. 29.

principles.name: Plenitude
principles.statement: Every total single-valued binary relation is represented by an operation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

principles.name: Possibility+ (pure)
principles.statement: The strengthened Possibility schema for pure C-consistent formulas whose only free variables are the displayed individual variables; include the empty tuple.
principles.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,(\bigwedge_{i<j}x_i\ne x_j)\to\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ C+P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60; Appendix E, p. 83.

references.locator: §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60; Appendix E, p. 83

principles.notes: The consistency and purity restrictions are inherited from Possibility, which the surrounding text says this strengthens; the shortened display on p. 41 must not be read as admitting contradictory P.

changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged. Renamed from “Possibility+” to mark it as the pure-language version, now that Possibility+ (signature Σ) is recorded; id and connections unchanged.

principles.name: Possibility+ (signature Σ)
principles.statement: The Possibility+ schema for the fixed nonlogical signature Sigma: for a formula P of L(Sigma) consistent with C(Sigma) whose free variables are the displayed individual variables, if those individuals are pairwise distinct and distinct from every individual denoted by a constant occurring in P, then P is possible. Include the empty tuple.
principles.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,\bigl(\bigwedge_{i<j}x_i\ne x_j\land\bigwedge_{i,\,c}x_i\ne c\bigr)\to\Diamond P\quad(P\in\mathcal L(\Sigma),\text{ free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ c\text{ over the individual constants in }P;\ C(\Sigma)+P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60, read with the signature convention of §2.5, pp. 37–39.

references.note: The draft states Possibility+ in the pure language; this is its analogue for L(Σ), added at Cian Dorr’s request to parallel Possibility (signature Σ).

principles.notes: The clause requiring the individuals to differ from the constants named in P is forced: without it the C(Σ)-consistent formula x ≠ c would yield ◇(c ≠ c).

principles.name: Possibility (pure)
principles.statement: Every closed pure sentence consistent with C is possible.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.4, pp. 35–36.

principles.name: Possibility (signature Σ)
principles.statement: The Possibility schema for the fixed nonlogical signature Sigma.
principles.formal: $\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ closed in }\mathcal L(\Sigma);\ C(\Sigma)+P\text{ consistent})$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 37–39.

principles.name: Possible Infinity (type e)
principles.statement: Possibly there are not finitely many individuals: the Axiom of Infinity at this type, under a diamond.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 20 September 2026.
principles.notes: Weaker than the Axiom of Infinity at this type by T. Since the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$ is consistent with C, Possibility (pure) implies this principle. With No Pure Contingency, or with BF, it gives the Axiom back; whether it does so in C alone is recorded as an open question. See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$.

principles.name: Possible Infinity (type t)
principles.statement: Possibly there are not finitely many propositions: the Axiom of Infinity at this type, under a diamond.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 20 September 2026.
principles.notes: Weaker than the Axiom of Infinity at this type by T. Since the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ is consistent with C, Possibility (pure) implies this principle, and indeed the Axiom itself by a longer route. With No Pure Contingency, or with BF (type $t$), this principle gives the Axiom back; whether it does so in C alone is recorded as an open question. See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$.

principles.name: Possibly Witnessed Possibility
principles.statement: For pure formulas P with free variables among a finite tuple x and distinct matching constants c, a possible witness to P entails that P at those constants is possible. Equivalently, P necessary at the constants is necessary universally.
principles.formal: $\Diamond(\exists\bar x\, .\,P)\to\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 38–39 and n. 57.

references.note: Separated Structure and Witnessed Possibility, between which this principle sits.
Separated Structure, to which this principle is equivalent in C.

principles.notes: Strengthens Witnessed Possibility by weakening its antecedent from an actual to a possible witness; its contrapositive is □P[c̄/x̄] → □∀x̄ P, the left-to-right direction of Logical Necessity with a box on the right. Equivalent in C to Separated Structure by the recorded results, so Logical Necessity is Separated Structure together with No Pure Contingency.

principles.name: B for pure sentences
principles.statement: The B instance for every closed sentence in the pure language.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, n. 81, p. 59.

principles.name: Relational Choice
principles.statement: Every serial binary relation has a functional subrelation.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\sigma,\tau\, .\,\forall U^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land(\forall x y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(Ux)y)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

principles.name: Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a rigid one.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\exists Y\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 28–30.

principles.name: Separated Structure
principles.statement: For each typed nonlogical constant c and closed same-typed terms F,G not containing c, equality after application to c implies equality of F and G.
principles.formal: $Fc=Gc\to F=G\quad(c\text{ a constant of }\Sigma;\ F,G\text{ closed, not containing }c)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 38–39.

references.note: Derived from Quantified Separated Structure and the assumptions Purity and Fundamentality; General Separated Structure on p. 565.

changes.summary: Added direct locators in Logical Combinatorialism; the statement is unchanged.
Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

principles.name: B for sentences of Σ
principles.statement: The B instance for every closed sentence of the language of the fixed signature Sigma.
principles.formal: $P\to\Box\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, n. 81, p. 59 (B for pure sentences).
Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §3, n. 32, p. 556.

references.note: Bacon’s observation that B for sentences with a nonlogical predicate is undermined by Witnessed Possibility independently of contingent distinctness.

principles.notes: Sits between B and B for pure sentences. Incompatible with Witnessed Possibility, unlike its pure counterpart, which Witnessed Possibility tolerates.

principles.name: Strong Leibniz Biconditionals
principles.statement: At each relational type, every possible entity (one distinct from bottom) is entailed by a strong world: a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation. The right-to-left direction is a theorem of C; the principle records the substantive direction.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\sigma\ne e\, .\,\forall X^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond_\sigma X\to\exists W^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SWorld}_\sigma(W)\land W\le_\sigma X$
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–166.
principles.notes: Bacon’s higher-order rendering of the possible-worlds thesis that a proposition is possible iff true at some world, with worlds required to settle merely possible propositions too. Definitions in Background. The book presents the connection between the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals and BF at relational types as new to it (§8.4, p. 177).

principles.name: Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t)
principles.statement: The type-t instance of the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals: every possible proposition is entailed by a strong world proposition, one that is possible and necessarily entails every proposition or its negation.
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–165.
principles.notes: Broken out as its own principle, like Atomicity (type t), at Cian Dorr’s request, because the type-t case can be settled in many models where the higher types have not been checked. In a one-object action model whose propositions are all the sets of arrows, every singleton is a strong world: seen from an arrow i, the singleton of h becomes the set of j with j∘i = h, and every proposition at that world is the shift of a root proposition, which cannot separate two such j. Multi-object models differ; see the two-object retract.

principles.name: Strong Possibility (pure)
principles.statement: Each closed pure sentence consistent with Maximalist Classicism is possible under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 42.
principles.notes: The paper leaves consistency open. The definition of Box_ne and its dual is given in Background. Whatever is consistent with Max(C) is already possible by Possibility (pure), which this principle implies; what it adds is possibility under the distinctness-preserving modality. So incompatibilities of the form Strong Possibility + □Y are recorded at Possibility (pure) and inherited, and the collapse is the one recorded principle refuted by the stronger modality alone.

principles.name: Strong Possibility (signature Σ)
principles.statement: Every closed sentence of the fixed signature consistent with its Maximalist Classicism is possible under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 37–39; §2.6, p. 42.
principles.notes: This keeps the signature-expanded reference theory throughout the consistency side condition. The separate pure-language variant uses Max(C). No conservativity between these two maximalizations is assumed. Consistency of Strong Possibility is left open in the source. Whatever is consistent with Max(C(Σ)) is already possible by Possibility (signature Σ), which this principle implies; what it adds is possibility under the distinctness-preserving modality. Incompatibilities of the form Strong Possibility (signature Σ) + □Y are inherited through Possibility (signature Σ) and Possibility (pure); the collapse is refuted directly.

principles.name: Tractarianism
principles.statement: A proposition entailing every instance of a property entails its universal generalization.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\sigma\, .\,\forall p^t X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,p\le Xx)\to p\le(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.1 and n. 27, pp. 20–21.

principles.name: Very Weak Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a very weakly rigid one, that is, with one that is weakly persistent and weakly inextensible.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\exists Y\, .\,\operatorname{VeryWeaklyRigid}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, p. 12.
Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.

references.note: The draft's unqualified "weakly rigid" is this map's very weakly rigid, the whole matrix of Rigid shorn of its leading box.

principles.notes: Very weak rigidity drops the leading box from both conjuncts of Rigid. See Background for the definitions. This is equivalent to Weak Rigid Comprehension, although very weak rigidity is strictly weaker than weak rigidity as a condition on a given relation.

principles.name: Weak Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a weakly rigid one, that is, with one that is persistent and weakly inextensible.
principles.formal: $\forall^{\mathrm{Ty}}\bar\sigma\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\exists Y\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, Proposition 1, p. 2; p. 12.

references.note: Source of Rigid Comprehension, of which this is the un-necessitated weakening.

principles.notes: Weak rigidity drops the leading box from the inextensibility conjunct of Rigid but keeps persistence in its necessitated form. See Background for the definitions. The draft that introduces the principle is a work in progress.

principles.name: Witnessed Possibility
principles.statement: For pure-formulas P with free variables among a finite tuple x, and distinct matching nonlogical constants c, a witness to P entails that P at those constants is possible.
principles.formal: $(\exists\bar x\, .\,P)\to\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, n. 57, p. 38.

references.locator: Logical Necessity discussion, as cited in Classicism n. 57

references.note: Bacon’s No Brute Necessities, Pattern and the recombination examples of §3 are this direction of Logical Necessity, with the Tarskian notion of consistency as an actual witness.

changes.summary: Added the alias No Brute Necessities and a direct locator in Logical Combinatorialism; the statement is unchanged.
Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, n. 31, p. 25.
results.proof: Specialize Actual Profile to the empty tuple, so its relation variables have type t.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, n. 31, p. 25.
results.proof: Let w witness Actuality. At a tuple $\bar x$, use the relation $\lambda\bar y\, .\,w\land\bigwedge_i x_i=y_i$. It holds at $\bar x$. If $Z[\bar x]$ is true, w entails that truth; NI preserves the tuple identities, so the proposed relation entails Z. This gives the required profile for every type tuple.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 38, p. 29.
results.proof: If w is the actual atom, the source takes $\lambda\bar y\, .\,w\land X[\bar y]$. Since w is true, this is coextensive with X. Its restriction to the actual complete profile makes the universal necessary consequences of its instances entailed by it, giving the source’s inextensibility condition.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 38, p. 29.
results.proof: If w witnesses Actuality, then $\lambda\bar y\, .\,w\le X[\bar y]$ is coextensive with X. Entailments are necessary when true, so this relation is persistent.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 25; Appendix D, p. 78 (Part 4).
results.proof:
Let $a$ be a strongest truth, as Actuality supplies. Since $a$ is true, $a
e ot$, so $\Diamond a$. Atomlessness then gives $q$ with $\Diamond q$, $q\le a$ and $q
e a$. If $q$ were true, Actuality would give $a\le q$, and with $q\le a$ antisymmetry gives $q=a$, contrary to $q
e a$. So $q$ is false, and $a\land
eg q$ is true, whence $a\le a\land
eg q\le
eg q$. Combined with $q\le a$ this gives $q\le
eg q$, so $q=q\land
eg q= ot$, contradicting $\Diamond q$. In short, a strongest truth is an atom.

references.note: The draft does not state the incompatibility, but its discussion of the Part 4 model observes that only the restriction of Atomlessness to false propositions can hold once the strongest truth is available.

results.notes: This explains why Atomlessness holds only in Parts 1–3 of Proposition D.5, since Parts 4, 5, 7 and 8 satisfy Actuality and Parts 6–8 satisfy Atomicity. The restriction of Atomlessness to false propositions, which the draft notes holds in Part 4, is not a principle of the map.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.7, p. 26.
results.proof: If w is a propositional atom, it entails every conditional $q\to(w\le q)$: either it entails q, in which case the entailment is necessary, or it entails its negation. Tractarianism, equivalent to BF, combines these into the universal claim that w entails every truth. Hence w entails Actuality. Atomicity says every possible proposition has an atom below it, so no possible proposition can entail the negation of Actuality. Thus that negation is $\bot$ and Actuality is necessary.

sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, Exercise 8.12, p. 166.
results.proof:
Let $W$ be a weak world of relational type $\sigma$: $W
e ot$ and $ orall Y\, .\,W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y$. We show $\Box orall Y\, .\,W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y$. Each instance is necessary once true, since $W\le Y$ is $\Box$ of a closed formula and 4 holds; so $ orall Y\, .\,\Box(W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y)$. BF at type $\sigma$ (the instance for the property $\lambda Y\, .\,W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y$) turns this into $\Box orall Y\, .\,W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y$. Thus every weak world is a strong world, and Atomicity supplies a weak world below each possible $X$.
results.notes: Bacon states this for relational types other than e, which is the map’s type range for both worlds principles; BF is used only at those types.

Tractarianism, equivalent to BF, combines these into the universal claim that w entails every truth. Hence w entails Actuality. Atomicity says every possible proposition has an atom below it, so no possible proposition can entail the negation of Actuality. Thus that negation is $\bot$ and Actuality is necessary.

results.proof:
Let $w$ be an atom below the possible $p$. For each $q$, $w\le q\lor w\le
eg q$ is true and, being a disjunction of two necessities, necessary by 4; so $ orall q\, .\,\Box(w\le q\lor w\le
eg q)$. BF (type t), for the property $\lambda q\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le
eg q$, gives $\Box orall q\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le
eg q$. With $\Diamond w$, which is $w

results.proof:
Call $q$ a floor of $X^{tt}$ when $Xq$, $\Diamond q$, and no possible instance of $X$ lies strictly below $q$. Let $W$ be the property of cardinalities holding of $Z$ when every instance of $Z$ that has a possible instance has a floor.

$W$ holds of $\mathbf{0}_t$, since its only instance has no instances at all, so the condition is vacuous.

$W$ is closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_t$. Let $WY$ and $(\operatorname{Suc}_t Y)X$, and take the witness $y$ with $Xy$ and $Y(\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y)$; write $X^-$ for that abstract, whose instances are exactly the instances of $X$ other than $y$. Suppose $X$ has a possible instance. If $X^-$ has none then $y$ is the only one, and is a floor. Otherwise the hypothesis on $Y$, applied to $X^-$ as $\operatorname{Suc}_t$ presents it, gives a floor $q$ of $X^-$. If $y$ is not possible, or is not strictly below $q$, then $q$ is a floor of $X$, since a possible instance of $X$ strictly below $q$ is either an instance of $X^-$, against the choice of $q$, or is $y$, which this case excludes. If instead $y$ is possible and strictly below $q$, then $y$ is a floor of $X$. For a possible instance $r$ of $X$ strictly below $y$ is not $y$, hence is an instance of $X^-$, and $r\le y\le q$. If $r=q$ then $q\le y\le q$ makes $y=q$, against $y\ne q$; so $r$ is an instance of $X^-$ strictly below $q$, again against the choice of $q$.

So every finite cardinality has the property. Now suppose some finite $Z$ held of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$. That property has the possible instance $\top$, since $\top\ne\bot$ in C, so it would have a floor $q$. Atomlessness applied to $q$ supplies a possible $q'$ with $q'\le q$ and $q'\ne q$, and $q'$ is an instance of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$, contradicting the floor. Hence no finite cardinality holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$.

references.note: Formulation of Atomlessness. The draft does not draw the connection.

results.notes: The induction stays inside the presentation that $\operatorname{Suc}_t$ supplies, applying the hypothesis to the abstract $\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y$ itself rather than to a coextensive property. That is what makes it go through without Extensionality. The recorded implication to the Infinity schema is a consequence of this one and is left in place as the shorter argument.

results.proof: In C the top and bottom propositions differ, so $\Diamond\top$. Atomlessness applied to $\top$ gives a possible $q_1$ with $q_1\le\top$ and $q_1\ne\top$; applied to $q_1$ it gives a possible $q_2$ strictly below $q_1$, and so on. After $n$ steps the chain $\top,q_1,\ldots,q_n$ descends strictly in the algebraic order, and a strictly descending chain in a partial order has pairwise distinct members. For if $q_i=q_j$ with $i<j$ then $q_i\le q_{i+1}$, since $q_j\le q_{i+1}$, while $q_{i+1}\le q_i$, so antisymmetry gives $q_{i+1}=q_i$, against the choice of $q_{i+1}$. Each instance of the Infinity schema therefore needs only finitely many applications of the single Atomlessness sentence.

results.proof:
Let $X$ be given and let $Y$ be a persistent coextension, which Persistent Comprehension supplies. Only persistence of $Y$ is used. What has to be added is that $
eg Y$ is persistent, which is the necessitation of a pointwise implication, so the argument must run at every world; that is what the boxed premise supplies. At any world, take $ ar x$ with $
eg Y[ ar x]$ and suppose $\Diamond Y[ ar x]$. Persistence of $Y$ is itself necessary, so $\Diamond Y[ ar x]$ yields $\Diamond\Box Y[ ar x]$. Boxed ND gives B at every world, and B in the form $\Diamond\Box p	o p$ then yields $Y[ ar x]$, against the assumption. So $\Box
eg Y[ ar x]$, which is persistence of $
eg Y$. Hence $Y$ is Gallin-extensional and coextensive with $X$.

references.note: The equivalence of ND with B, and the Gallin convention.

results.notes: Rigid Comprehension implies Persistent Comprehension, so this covers the reading on which rigidity yields Gallin-extensionality. The boxed form of ND is needed rather than the plain form, because persistence of the negation is itself a boxed claim and the argument has to be available at every world. In the other direction the draft's note uses BF, which is doing separate work: it stops a world from having instances that the base world does not supply, and no amount of ND replaces it.

results.proof:
Fix a relational type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ and $X^\tau$. Write $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\bigwedge_i z_i=u_i$ and put $H:=\lambda Z^\tau\, .\,\exists\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\land Z=\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar y}$, the property of being the haecceity of some $X$ things. By Boolean Completeness in its least-upper-bound form, let $Y$ be a least upper bound of $H$. Two observations do the work. (i) If $X[\bar u]$ then $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}\le_\tau Y$, and instantiating at $\bar u$ with $\bar u=\bar u$ gives $\Box Y[\bar u]$. (ii) If $\Box Z[\bar u]$ whenever $X[\bar u]$, then $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}\le_\tau Z$ for each such $\bar u$, so $Z$ is an upper bound of $H$ and $Y\le_\tau Z$.

Coextensiveness. $X[\bar u]\to Y[\bar u]$ by (i). Conversely, let $w$ witness Actuality and put $P:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,(w\le X[\bar z])$. If $X[\bar u]$ then $X[\bar u]$ is true, so $w\le X[\bar u]$; a true entailment is necessary, so $\Box P[\bar u]$. By (ii), $Y\le_\tau P$, so $Y[\bar u]\to w\le X[\bar u]$; and $w$ is true, so $Y[\bar u]\to X[\bar u]$.

Persistence. Take $Z:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]$ in (ii). If $X[\bar u]$ then $\Box Y[\bar u]$ by (i), hence $\Box Z[\bar u]$ by 4. So $Y\le_\tau\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]$, which is $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)$.

Weak inextensibility. Suppose $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to\Box Z[\bar z]$. If $X[\bar u]$ then $Y[\bar u]$ by coextensiveness, so $\Box Z[\bar u]$; hence $Y\le_\tau Z$ by (ii).

references.note: Boolean Completeness and Actuality; the least-upper-bound form of Boolean Completeness is equivalent to the stated greatest-lower-bound form in C.

results.notes: The argument stops short of Rigid Comprehension exactly at the leading box of Inextensible. It delivers a $Y$ that is inextensible at the actual world, while Rigid demands the biconditional at every world. The models recorded from the same draft show that the gap is real.

results.proof: Theorem 9 of the source, proved in HKC, which C extends. Natural numberhood is necessary (Lemma 3, an induction using the converse Barcan formula), distinct numbers are necessarily distinct given $I^*$ (Lemma 4, a double induction), $I$ implies $I^*$ (Lemma 5), so distinctness and, by tedious inductions, Sum and Prod are necessary or necessarily false given $I$ (Lemmas 6–7). Countable Boolean Completeness is used once, in Lemma 8: the property of being a singleton of a number is countable, so it has a least upper bound $B$; $B$ necessarily holds of every number, so the property of being the successor of a $B$ is also an upper bound, hence $B$ necessitates it, and induction gives that necessarily every number is a $B$; thus any property necessarily had by each number is necessarily had by every number. Theorem 9 then proceeds by induction on arithmetical formulas, Lemma 8 handling the restricted universal quantifier. See the write-up.
results.notes: Lemma 3 of the source is the persistence of being a finite cardinality, Lemma 1 of the write-up for pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t. Lemma 8 says that natural numberhood is a rigid property in the source's sense, the Barcan direction; the converse Barcan direction is Lemma 3. e}p$, there is a true $q$ with $\Box(\Diamond q	o p)$; $q$ true gives $q
e ot$, and ND at type $t$ gives $\Box(q
e ot)$, that is $\Box\Diamond q$; K then gives $\Box p$. So the collapse yields $ orall p\, .\,p	o\Box p$: every truth is $	op$. Then materially equivalent propositions are identical: if both are true both are $	op$; if both are false their negations are $	op$, so both are $ ot$. That is the Fregean Axiom.

results.proof: Let $c$ be a constant of type $\sigma$ and $F,G$ closed terms of type $\sigma\tau$ not containing $c$, with $Fc=Gc$. Enumerate the constants occurring in $F$ or $G$ as $\bar d$, all distinct from $c$, and abstract them: $F=F^\circ\bar d$, $G=G^\circ\bar d$ with $F^\circ,G^\circ$ closed and pure, by $\beta$. Let $P:=F^\circ\bar y\,x=G^\circ\bar y\,x$, pure with free variables $\bar y,x$. NI gives $\Box P[\bar d,c/\bar y,x]$, so Logical Necessity, left to right, gives $\forall\bar y x\, .\,P$. This closed pure truth is necessary by the empty-tuple instance of Logical Necessity, so $\Box\forall\bar y x\, .\,F^\circ\bar y x=G^\circ\bar y x$. CBF gives $\forall\bar y\, .\,\Box\forall x\, .\,F^\circ\bar yx=G^\circ\bar yx$ and Modalized Functionality, a theorem of C, gives $\forall\bar y\, .\,F^\circ\bar y=G^\circ\bar y$. Instantiating $\bar y:=\bar d$ yields $F=G$.
results.notes: Bacon derives the quantified form from Quantified Logical Necessity and Modalized Functionality and says the schematic form follows in the same way. Both directions of Logical Necessity are used: the witnessed direction to pass from the necessary identity at the constants to the universal claim, and No Pure Contingency to necessitate that claim before applying Modalized Functionality.

results.proof: For a relation X, form the property F of haecceities of its instances and take their least upper bound $X^*$. It contains each X-instance. Actuality follows from Atomicity and BF by Proposition 2.7; let w be the actual atom. The relation $w\to X$ is an upper bound of F, so $X^*$ is also contained in X. Each haecceity entails its own necessitation by NI, so $\Box X^*$ is another upper bound; hence $X^*$ is persistent. For inextensibility, note 42 assumes a possible failure, uses boxed Atomicity and BF to obtain atoms w and w′ witnessing the two stages, and replaces w′ by the GLB of its w-possible aliases. Then $w^{\prime}\to Y$ is an upper bound of F but is contradicted by the proposed failure of inextensibility. This contradiction establishes rigidity.
results.notes: This is a summary of note 42; see the accompanying write-up for the alias-GLB step. The source’s first cross-reference to Proposition 2.6 is replaced in this transcription by the sufficient Proposition 2.7; the statement and premises are unchanged.

sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, Theorem 8.2, pp. 169–171.
results.proof: Theorem 8.2 of the book: given Rigid Comprehension, $\Box\mathrm{SL}_\sigma$ at all relational types implies $\Box\mathrm{BF}_\sigma$ for every relational $\sigma\ne e$. Its proof for $\sigma=t$ (pp. 170–171): from $\Diamond\exists p\, .\,Xp$, $X$ is a possible property, so by $\mathrm{SL}_{tt}$ it is entailed by a strong world property $W$; let $H$ be the rigid collection, supplied by Rigid Comprehension, of world properties accessible to $W$, and let $r:=\exists V\, .\,\exists p\, .\,HV\land Vp\land p$. Bacon shows $\Box\forall p\, .\,Wp\to p=r$, using $\Box\mathrm{SL}_t$ for the step that every world proposition entails $\exists V\, .\,HV\land Vp$ and the rigidity of $H$ for the converse; since $W$ entails $X$, $\Diamond Xr$, which gives $\exists p\, .\,\Diamond Xp$, the contrapositive of $\mathrm{BF}_t$. The argument is carried out under necessary assumptions, so it yields $\Box\mathrm{BF}_t$. The map records the type-$t$ instance; the book proves the same for every relational type other than $e$.
results.notes: The map has no node for BF restricted to relational types, so the conclusion is recorded at type t, the case the book proves in full. The right-to-left half of Theorem 8.2 is the recorded implication from □Atomicity and □BF to □SL, which needs no Rigid Comprehension.

results.proof:
Let $c$ be a constant of $\Sigma$ of some relational type $	au$. The pure formulas $x=	op_	au$ and $x
e	op_	au$ have witnesses, so Witnessed Possibility gives $\Diamond(c=	op_	au)$ and $\Diamond(c
e	op_	au)$. By excluded middle one of the closed $\Sigma$-sentences $c=	op_	au$, $c
e	op_	au$ is true, and No Contingency (signature Σ) makes it necessary, contradicting the possibility of the other.
results.notes: Hence No Contingency (signature Σ) excludes Logical Necessity, Separated Structure, Possibly Witnessed Possibility and Maximalist Classicism for Σ, while it is consistent with No Pure Contingency and holds in every one-world model.

results.proof: Every closed instance of Actuality is a closed sentence of the pure language, since the principle is stated with object-language quantifiers and contains no nonlogical constant. Given Actuality, each of those instances is true, and No Pure Contingency makes a true closed pure sentence necessary. So every closed instance is necessary, which is what the boxed principle asserts. Any type range and side conditions stay outside the box, as the Modal scope convention requires.

references.note: Formulation of No Pure Contingency. The draft does not draw this consequence.

results.notes: One of a uniform family. No Pure Contingency carries any pure principle of the map to its boxed form, because a boxed principle here says exactly that each closed instance of the base is necessary. The argument turns on the base being stated with quantifiers rather than as a schema over arbitrary formulas, since an instance carrying a nonlogical constant would fall outside No Pure Contingency.

results.proof:
Theorem 11 of the source, applied to C. The theorems of C are recursively enumerable, and C is consistent with $I$, since $I^*$ and hence $I$ hold in the full Henkin model with a countably infinite individual domain. So the arithmetical sentences $A$ with $C\vdash I	o A$ form a consistent, recursively enumerable extension of Peano arithmetic (the source's Lemma 1 supplies the axioms). By Gödel's first incompleteness theorem there is an arithmetical sentence $A$ for which neither $I	o A$ nor $I	o
eg A$ is a theorem of C, so $I\land A$ and $I\land
eg A$ are both consistent with C. Both are closed pure sentences, so Possibility (pure) gives $\Diamond(I\land A)$ and $\Diamond(I\land
eg A)$. But the instance of the Necessity of Arithmetic at $A$ says $\Box(I	o A)$ or $\Box(I	o
eg A)$, and by K each disjunct contradicts one of the two possibilities.
results.notes: The source's theorem is general: the maximalization of any recursively enumerable extension of HK consistent with $I$ refutes some instance of the necessity schema. The record uses Possibility (pure) directly; the equivalent Distinctness form gives the same through the recorded equivalence. The argument is metatheoretic in two places, the recursive enumerability of C and Gödel's theorem, like the consistency side condition of Possibility itself.

results.proof: Let $P$ be a closed pure sentence consistent with C. By the completeness half of Classicism, Theorem 3.23, some action model makes $P$ true. An action model carries an interpretation of the nonlogical constants (Definition 3.25 refers to it), and the frame with any interpretation of the constants of Σ in the domains of their types, nonempty by Existence, is again an action model, in which $P$ remains true, $P$ containing no constants. By the soundness half of the same theorem, applied to the language $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$, every theorem of C(Σ) is true in it. So $P$ is consistent with C(Σ), and Possibility (signature Σ) gives $\Diamond P$.

references.note: Soundness and completeness of action models, and the action-model interpretation of nonlogical constants.

results.notes: Records that the signature-expanded reference theory is conservative over C for pure sentences, which is what the arrow from the Σ form of Possibility to the pure form needs. The analogous arrow between the two Strong Possibility principles remains conjectured, since it needs the conservativity of Max(C(Σ)) over Max(C), which this argument does not give: a model of Max(C) with the constants interpreted arbitrarily need not satisfy the possibility of every C(Σ)-consistent Σ-sentence.

Let $H:=\lambda\bar x\, .\,(F\bar x=G\bar x)$, closed and pure. If $F\bar c=G\bar c$ then NI gives $\Box(F\bar c=G\bar c)$, i.e. $\Box H\bar c$ by $\beta$. results.proof:
For $k\ge1$ let $E_k$ be the closed pure sentence saying that there are exactly $k$ individuals, $\exists x_1^e\cdots x_k^e\, .\,( igwedge_{i<j}x_i
e x_j)\land orall y^e\, .\, igvee_i y=x_i$. Fix $n$ and take $E_1,\ldots,E_n$. For $i
e j$ the identity $E_i=E_j$ is closed and pure, and C does not prove it. A full Henkin model whose individual domain has exactly $i$ members is a model of C in which $E_i$ is true and $E_j$ is false, and at type $t$ that model's propositions are its two truth values, so the two sentences denote different things there. Distinctness therefore gives $E_i
e E_j$. So $E_1,\ldots,E_n$ are $n$ pairwise distinct propositions, which is the $n$-th instance of Infinity at type $t$.

references.note: Formulations of Distinctness and Infinity, and the full Henkin models that supply the non-theoremhood side condition. The draft does not draw the connection between them.

results.notes:
Recorded from Distinctness because the proof uses its non-theoremhood side condition directly. The equivalent Possibility form gives the same result through the recorded equivalence. The witnesses need not be possible propositions, and at most one of them is true. What Distinctness supplies is that C proves no identity among them. Only the type-$t$ instance follows, since the witnesses are propositions about how many individuals there are, not individuals.

The argument does not lift to the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$, and it is worth recording how far it does reach. For each fixed $k$ it refutes the claim that there are exactly $k$ propositions. If there were, then among the $k+1$ sentences $E_1,\ldots,E_{k+1}$ two would have to coincide, so C proves the finite disjunction of those identities, and Distinctness refutes every disjunct. That is the schema over again, one sentence at a time. The axiom asks for the same of every cardinality falling under $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$, including ones that no closed term names, and Distinctness bears only on identities between closed pure terms, so it says nothing about the domain over which $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$ quantifies. Any one derivation uses finitely many of its instances, and those are satisfiable while the universal property still carries a cardinality that the induction clause admits. The route through Atomlessness is closed too, since the map carries a model of the signature Distinctness schema that satisfies Actuality, and Actuality excludes Atomlessness.

Added 20 September 2026: a different argument does reach the axiom. Applying the consistency side condition once, to the single sentence that every finite cardinality has a possibly instantiated successor, gives that sentence outright by persistence, and from it the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ follows in C; see pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t. The limits described above concern the numeral-by-numeral argument recorded here.

results.proof: Write $g(Z)$ for $(\operatorname{Suc}_e Z)(\lambda x^e\, .\,\top)$ and let $\Pi$ be the closed pure sentence $\forall Z^{(et)t}\, .\,\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_e(Z)\to\Diamond g(Z)$: there could be any positive number of individuals. Zero must be left out, since Existence makes $\mathbf{0}_e(\lambda x\, .\,\top)$ identical to $\bot$. $\Pi$ is true at the root of the model coalesced-all-finite-individual-domains, so it is consistent with C and Possibility gives $\Diamond\Pi$. Being a finite cardinality is persistent, and the defined necessity satisfies 4, so $\Diamond\Pi$ yields $\Pi$ itself. Under $\Pi$ the map $g$ is injective on finite cardinalities: two finite cardinalities are either identical or necessarily share no instance, by an induction that stays inside the presentation $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ supplies, and the second disjunct is excluded when the two values of $g$ coincide and are possible. Hence the propositions $g(Z)$, $Z$ finite, carry a copy of the successor structure: the relation taking $g(Z)$ to $g(\operatorname{Suc}_e Z)$, and every other proposition to itself, is total and injective on $\lambda p\, .\,\top$ and misses $g(\mathbf{0}_e)$. A property with such a relation has no finite cardinality, by induction on the cardinality. So no finite cardinality of type $(tt)t$ holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$. The full proof, with the six lemmas, is in the write-up.

results.notes: Recorded from Possibility because the proof applies its consistency side condition to one sentence, $\Pi$, which quantifies over every finite cardinality at once. results.proof:
Let $Y$ be very weakly rigid and coextensive with $X$, and put $Y':=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]$.

Coextensiveness. $\Box Y[\bar u]\to Y[\bar u]$ by T, and $Y[\bar u]\to\Box Y[\bar u]$ is $\operatorname{WeaklyPersistent}(Y)$. So $Y'$ is coextensive with $Y$, hence with $X$.

Persistence. $Y'\le\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y'[\bar z]$ is $\Box\forall\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]\to\Box\Box Y[\bar z]$, the necessitation of the 4 axiom, which is a theorem of C.

Weak inextensibility. Suppose $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y'[\bar z]\to\Box Z[\bar z]$. Weak persistence gives $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to Y'[\bar z]$, so $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to\Box Z[\bar z]$, and $\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)$ gives $Y\le Z$. Also $Y'\le Y$, since that is the necessitation of T. So $Y'\le Z$ by transitivity.

Hence $Y'$ is weakly rigid and coextensive with $X$.

results.proof: Take the propositional case first. Given $F^{tt}$, let $C^{tt}$ be weakly rigid and coextensive with $F$, and put $q:=\exists p\, .\,Cp\land p$. Every $F$ proposition $p$ is $C$, hence necessarily $C$ by persistence, so $p$ entails $Cp\land p$ and thereby $q$; so $q$ is an upper bound of the $F$ propositions. Now suppose every $F$ proposition entails $r$. The $C$ propositions are the $F$ propositions, so every $C$ proposition entails $r$; entailments are necessary if true, so $\forall p\, .\,Cp\to\Box(p\le r)$. Weak inextensibility with $X:=\lambda p\, .\,(p\le r)$ gives $C\le X$, so at every world $Cp$ implies $p\le r$; hence $Cp\land p$ entails $r$ whatever $p$ may be, and $q\le r$. So $q$ is a least upper bound of the $F$ propositions. The same reasoning with extra parameters gives the least-upper-bound form at every relational type, and that form is equivalent in C to the greatest-lower-bound form in which the principle is stated.

models.description: Take the full Henkin models $M_n$ with individual domain $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ for every $n\ge1$, and add a root world. Individuals are threads $(a_n)_n$ with $a_n\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$; propositions are sets of worlds; an entity of a function type is a family of $M_n$-entities together with an arbitrary root component defined on whole threads. Application is componentwise, identity at world $n$ is the identity of $M_n$ and at the root is identity of elements. Every theorem of C holds at every world. At the root the finite cardinalities are the numerals, the $k$-th numeral's successor holds of the universal property at world $k+1$, and $\Diamond$ at the root is truth at some world, so the sentence that there could be any positive number of individuals, used in pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t, holds there. The root has uncountably many individuals and infinitely many propositions, so both Axioms of Infinity hold there. Two threads that agree at some world are distinct but possibly identical, so ND fails at type $e$. Evaluation point: the root.

models.description: For a signature Σ with countably infinitely many individual constants and at least one relational constant, take a set of action models for L(Σ) complete for C(Σ), and coalesce them at a new root whose individual domain is the set of individual constants, each constant denoting itself there and being carried by the distinguished arrow to each component onto its interpretation in that component; relational constants are glued as in Definition E.2, with free root extensions. Evaluation point: the root.
models.notes:
The root satisfies Maximalist Classicism for Σ, since every C(Σ)-consistent sentence holds at some component root. It satisfies Possibility+ (signature Σ): for P with free individual variables x̄, instantiate x̄ by pairwise distinct root individuals, that is, distinct constants c̄′ not occurring in P; P[c̄′/x̄] is C(Σ)-consistent because the c̄′ are fresh, so it is possible at the root. The instances of the pure form follow. Distinct constants denote distinct root individuals, so there are infinitely many individuals at the root, giving the Infinity Schema at type e and, the root domains being as full as possible so that the numeral intensions exist, the Axiom of Infinity at type e. Actuality holds by the singleton root proposition, and the p. 83 discussion of the distinctness-preserving collapse and the obstruction to Strong Possibility applies to this root as to the maximalist one. BF fails at the root. C is complete for the component set, so some component $M$ refutes BF at its root $M_0$, at type $t$ say: some $F$ in $M_0$’s domain has $ orall y\, .\,\Box Fy$ true and $\Diamond\exists y\, .\,
eg Fy$ true at $M_0$. Because the root’s domains are as full as possible, the thread $F^{\prime}$ that is universal at the root and in every other component and is carried onto $F$ by the distinguished arrow to $M_0$ is in the root domain. Every arrow from the root into $M$ factors through that distinguished arrow, so $ orall y\, .\,\Box F^{\prime}y$ at the root reduces to $ orall y\, .\,\Box Fy$ at $M_0$ together with trivial checks elsewhere, and $\Diamond\exists y\, .\,
eg F^{\prime}y$ at the root follows from $\Diamond\exists y\, .\,
eg Fy$ at $M_0$ through the same factorization. Observation of Cian Dorr, 22 September 2026. Root domains are as full as compatibility allows: a root proposition is a choice, for each component, of a proposition of that component’s root domain, together with a truth value at the root’s identity arrow, and a root entity of a relational type is likewise a family of component entities with a root component that is an arbitrary function of the root arguments. Atomicity fails at type t: C is complete for the components, so some component $M$ refutes Atomicity at its root, by a proposition $p_M$ with no atom below it in $M$’s domain; the root proposition that is $p_M$ on $M$, empty on every other component and false at the root has as its root lower bounds exactly the root propositions that are lower bounds of $p_M$ on $M$ and empty elsewhere, so it has no atom below it either. Boolean Completeness fails, at type $e	o t$, for the same reason: a component $M$ refutes it by a property $X_M$ of propositions without a greatest lower bound in $M$’s domain, and the root property holding of a root proposition iff $X_M$ holds of its $M$-component has no greatest lower bound at the root, since such a bound’s $M$-component would be one for $X_M$. Relational Choice holds at the root, contrary to a first guess: the functionality of a subrelation is evaluated at the root’s identity arrow only, while the subrelation condition is boxed; so for a serial root relation take the subrelation whose root component is a functional choice from the root component, by choice in the metatheory, and whose component parts are empty. Its necessitation fails, since some component refutes Relational Choice at its root. Possibility+ holds here, unlike at the maximalist root, because the root individuals are the constants, and two distinct constants stay distinct in every component where the sentence of their distinctness is realized, not in one component only. □Relational Choice fails, as the notes on Relational Choice explain: some component refutes Relational Choice at its root, which is accessible from the root.  Correction of 23 September 2026: the components are only known to refute Boolean Completeness at type $e	o t$ (Classicism, n. 92, conjectures failures at type $t$ but has none), so the transfer argument refutes the type schema of Boolean Completeness at the root, not its type-$t$ instance, which is left unknown; the same transfer, applied to the countable family of haecceities that witnesses the component failure, refutes Countable Boolean Completeness.  Boolean Completeness fails at type $t$ (restoring the claim corrected earlier in the day): the truncation model of Appendix D, part 6, refutes it at type $t$, as its record now shows, and the components are complete for C, so one of them does; the root propositions false at every arrow except those into that component form a copy of its propositional domain under the root’s entailment order, and a root property of propositions holding exactly of the copies of the members of that component’s counterexample family has no least upper bound at the root. Cian Dorr’s argument, 23 September 2026.

models.name: Finite-support action model: dyadic roundings of N
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix D, Proposition D.5, part 7, pp. 74, 78; p. 79 (No Pure Contingency).

references.locator: Appendix D, Proposition D.5(7), pp. 74–75; construction p. 78, Part 7; p. 79 (No Pure Contingency)

models.description: Proposition D.5, part 7 (p. 78): the arrows are the maps $f_n$, for $n$ a power of $2$, sending $m$ to the greatest multiple of $n$ not exceeding $m$; $f_1$ is the identity. Actuality and Atomicity hold because each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set ($\{n-2,n-1,n\}$ for $n>1$, $\{0,1\}$ for the identity); BF fails since an arrow sending $1$ to $0$ sends everything to even numbers; Boolean Completeness fails because the strongest persistent property with extension $\mathbb N$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ has, at $f_m$, the multiples of $\min\{m,n\}$ as extension and so becomes ever stronger. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of individuals (it is pinned down by that set), an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense, and the individuals are the natural numbers acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many individuals and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.
models.notes: The cited construction is a model of the map’s relational-type framework. The description identifies its evaluation point; construction and verification are given at the PDF locations in References. Boxed positive flags use the source’s explicit one-object No Pure Contingency observation, applied separately to each closed instance. Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition described above; every other relational constant denotes the top element of its type and every individual constant one fixed individual. Under it: No Contingency (signature Σ) fails, since the Σ-sentence $\forall\bar x\, .\,c\bar x$ denotes $a$, true and contingent; B for sentences of Σ fails, since under any arrow that no arrow composes back into $a$, $\Diamond a$ is false, so $\Box\Diamond a$ fails; Witnessed Possibility fails for the pure formula $x=\top_\tau$, witnessed by $\top_\tau$, since $\Diamond(c=\top_\tau)$ is $\Diamond\Box a$ and $a$ is necessary at no arrow; Separated Structure fails with it, being equivalent to Possibly Witnessed Possibility; Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness (signature Σ) fail through the other relational constants, Σ being assumed to contain at least one: such a constant $c'$ of type $\tau'$ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_{\tau'}$ denotes, and $c'=\top_{\tau'}$ is a true identity that C(Σ) does not prove. The designated constant refutes neither: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow (Classicism, §3.5, p. 58), whereas $a$ is fixed by no arrow but the identity, so no closed pure term denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$. Everything that implies these fails with them. Countable Boolean Completeness fails as well, at type $e\to t$: the property $E$ that the source shows to lack a least upper bound has as its extension a countable family of haecceities, and the extensional fullness the source invokes to put $E$ in the domain also puts in the relation pairing the haecceity of the $k$-th member of that family with the numeral $k$, which injects $E$ into the numerals. Observation of 23 September 2026. Distinctness-preserving collapse holds: for a true proposition $p$ pinned down by a finite set take as the witness $q$ the actual-world proposition $\{f_1\}$: under $f_n$ with $n>1$, $\Diamond q$ would need $k\circ f_n$ to be the identity, impossible since $f_n$ is not injective. Relational Choice holds, necessarily. models.description: Proposition D.5, part 3 (p. 77): the one-object category whose arrows are all the monotone maps of $\mathbb N$. models.name: Finite-support action model: qualitative contrast
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix D, p. 79, final construction (two copies of N).

references.locator: Appendix D, p. 79, final construction (two copies of N)

models.description: Appendix D, p. 79, the final construction: two objects $W_0$ and $W_1$, both copies of $\mathbb N$, with the permutations of $\mathbb N$ as the arrows between any pair of objects, finite subsets as $W_i^\ddagger$, and one constraint beyond ideal fullness: a set of arrows belongs to $W_i^t$ only if, whenever it contains an arrow $h$ into $W_0$, it contains $g\circ h$ for every permutation $g$ of $W_0$. Intuitively $W_0$ is a state in which all individuals are qualitatively indiscernible and $W_1$ one in which each plays a unique role. The smallest proposition of $W_0^t$ containing the identity is the set of all arrows $W_0\to W_0$, which witnesses Actuality at $W_0$; Actuality fails at $W_1$ as in part 1, so $\Box$Actuality and hence Atomicity fail at $W_0$ although C5 holds. Evaluation point: $W_0$, at its identity arrow.

The description identifies its evaluation point; construction and verification are given at the PDF locations in References. Under it the signature schemata fail. Let $c\in\Sigma$ have relational type $\tau$, so $c=\top_\tau$ necessarily. Witnessed Possibility fails for the pure formula $x\ne\top_\tau$, witnessed by $\bot_\tau$ but impossible of $c$; Separated Structure fails since $\lambda x\, .\,x$ and $\lambda x\, .\,\top_\tau$ agree on $c$ and differ; Independence (signature Σ) fails since $c$ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_\tau$ denotes; Distinctness (signature Σ) fails since $c=\top_\tau$ is a true identity that C(Σ) does not prove. Everything that implies these fails with them. models.name: Finite-support action model: truncated shifts of N
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix D, Proposition D.5, part 8, pp. 74, 78–79; p. 79 (No Pure Contingency).

references.locator: Appendix D, Proposition D.5(8), pp. 74–75; construction pp. 78–79, Part 8; p. 79 (No Pure Contingency)

models.description: Proposition D.5, part 8 (pp. 78–79): the arrows are the maps $k_n$ with $k_nm=0$ for $m\le n$ and $k_nm=m-n$ otherwise, which compose as $k_n\circ k_m=k_{n+m}$; $k_0$ is the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of individuals (it is pinned down by that set), an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense, and the individuals are the natural numbers acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many individuals and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

models.description: Let M be the free monoid of finite sequences of natural numbers under concatenation; its induced Kripke frame is the infinitely branching tree with the initial-segment relation and the empty sequence as root. Take the standard model over this frame (propositions all sets of accessible worlds, function types all homomorphisms) whose individuals at a world are the functions from the infinite branches through that world to the natural numbers, with restriction as counterpart; equivalently, the full action model over M with this surjective M-set at type e. This higher-order frame is isomorphic to the coalesced sum of countably many copies of itself, so coalesced sums of Σ-models over it are again Σ-models over it. Enumerate the Σ-sentences satisfiable in some Σ-model over the frame, choose a model of each, and glue them by the book’s Definition 18.15. Evaluation point: the root. The write-up carries the full verification.
models.notes: Promoted from conjectured on 22 September 2026. The gap in the source was its Theorem A.8, stated without proof, and the deferred type-e case; the write-up closes both by choosing a self-similar individual domain and applying the book’s coalesced sums. The signature is assumed countable; for a larger signature use a tree with as many branches. Distinct constants of one type denote distinct entities at the root, since every domain, including the individuals, has more than one element; they are also possibly identical. ND and B fail at type t already. Possibility (pure) fails because Actuality is necessary while its negation is consistent with C. Everything else follows from the listed principles by the map’s results. Bacon’s interpretation of his predicates Pure and Fun in this model, and the principles stated with them, are not recorded, following Zachary Goodsell’s decision to keep the map to the logical vocabulary and the constants of Σ. □Relational Choice holds: every truncation is a standard model over a frame isomorphic to the original, and Relational Choice holds in every full model given choice in the metatheory. Distinctness-preserving collapse holds: let $a$ be the proposition true at the actual world alone (the identity arrow). For any true $p$, take $q:=a$ in the definition of $\Box_{\ne}p$: under a non-identity arrow $i$, $\Diamond a$ would need an arrow $k$ with $k\circ i$ the identity, and none exists, since no arrow leads back to the actual world; under the identity, $p$ holds. So every truth is $\Box_{\ne}$-necessary, although ND fails.
